+        Fix: (Christophe Simon) OSX (darwin) platform detection

+        Fix: (Olivier Hanesse) #1845 Add missing paramter for statsd
+        Fix: (Nicolas Le Manchet) Improve systemd units reliability

+import javax.servlet.ServletContextEvent;
+import javax.servlet.ServletContextListener;
+

+ */
+public class KarafTerminalContextListener implements ServletContextListener {
+
+  private ConfigManager configManager = new ConfigManager();
+
+  @Override
+  public void contextInitialized(ServletContextEvent sce) {
+    try {
+      configManager.init();
+    } catch (Exception e) {
+      throw createServletException(e);
+    }
+    sce.getServletContext().setAttribute("ConfigManager", configManager);

+    try {

+    } catch (Exception e) {

+
+  }

+    return new RuntimeException(e);
+  }
+
+}

+
+### Problem
+
+[Security advisory](https://github.com/dapr/dapr/security/advisories/GHSA-59m6-82qm-vqgj)
+
+A high-severity vulnerability has been found in Dapr that allows bypassing [API token authentication](https://docs.dapr.io/operations/security/api-token/), which is used by the Dapr sidecar to authenticate calls coming from the application, with a well-crafted HTTP request.

+### Impact

+The vulnerability impacts all users on Dapr <=1.10.9 and <=1.11.2 who are using API token authentication.

+### Root cause

+The Dapr sidecar allowed all requests containing `/healthz` in the URL (including query string) to bypass API token authentication.
+
+### Solution
+
+We have changed the API token authentication middleware to allow bypassing the authentication only for healthcheck endpoints more strictly.

explanation:
Fixed API token authentication bypassed when path contains `/healthz`

The APITokenAuthMiddleware allowed bypassing the check if the path included `/healthz`. An attacker only needed to include `/healthz` in the URL, even the querystring, to bypass the API token check, for example `/v1.0/invoke/myapp/method/something?foo=/healthz`.

Additionally, this was not checking the method of the request, so requests to `POST /healthz` would cause a service invocation to happen.

This fixes the issue by making the check a lot more strict. The API token check can be bypassed only if:

- The path is exactly `/v1.0/healthz` or `/v1.0/healthz/outbound` (slashes are trimmed on each side)
- The method is `GET`

Fix user privilege escalation bug (#13976)

The AddUser() API endpoint was accepting a policy field. 
This API is used to update a user's secret key and account 
status, and allows a regular user to update their own secret key. 

The policy update is also applied though does not appear to 
be used by any existing client-side functionality.

This fix changes the accepted request body type and removes 
the ability to apply policy changes as that is possible via the 
policy set API.

NOTE: Changing passwords can be disabled as a workaround
for this issue by adding an explicit "Deny" rule to disable the API
for users.

[SECURITY] Respect expiration time of password reset token

When a TYPO3 backend user performs a password reset request, a
password reset link including an expiration time is sent to the
user. The expiration time is included in HMAC calculation of
the saved password reset hash, but it is never evaluated if the
expiration time is exceeded.

This change adds the missing validity check for the expiration
time included in the password reset link.

explanation:
[SECURITY] Limit user session to cookie domain

Given that there are two sites `site-a.com` and `site-b.com` in
the same TYPO3 installation, it was possible to reuse a session
cookie that was generated for `site-a.com` in `site-b.com`.

Since there are scenarios, where this is the expected behavior
– when sharing sessions across sub domains, so that an explicit
cookieDomain needs to be configured – user sessions signatures
are now salted with the desired cookie domain, so that a cookie
can only be used on the domain that the cookie was created for.

Testing framework will need to be adapted in a subsequent patch,
but for the time being – and for compatiblity with possible 3rd
party authenticators – legacy tokens will be accepted, but not
created by TYPO3 core.

fix: critical auth bug on pay-app acknowledge + add security headers + fix hydration

Three items in one commit because they're related hardening
that's safer to ship together than in three pieces.

================================================================
ITEM 1: Tenant isolation — /api/pay-apps/[id]/acknowledge
================================================================

Bug (CRITICAL): The public pay-app acknowledge endpoint had
ZERO authentication. Anyone with any payAppId could mark any
pay app as acknowledged by hitting:
  POST /api/pay-apps/<payAppId>/acknowledge
with an empty JSON body.

The intent was that the public /pay-apps/[token] page would
POST to this endpoint when the recipient clicked 'I
acknowledge this draw'. The page is reached via a token
link, no auth required. But the API route never verified
the share token — it just took the payAppId from the URL
and updated the pay app.

This is a cross-pay-app (and effectively cross-tenant)
vulnerability. Knowing one pay app's id (or guessing a
CUID, which is feasible) let you acknowledge any pay app.

Fix: the route now requires a shareToken in the request
body, looks up the pay app by shareToken (NOT by id), and
verifies the URL's payAppId matches the looked-up pay app's
id. Without a valid token: 404. With a valid token but
wrong payAppId: 404 (we don't leak whether the token
exists). With a valid token + matching payAppId: 200.

Also added:
- acknowledgedByEmail / acknowledgedByName on PayApp so
  we record who acknowledged (the previous code didn't
  capture the email the user typed)
- zod validation of the request body (was parsing
  untyped JSON, so a malformed body would 500 the worker)
- Idempotency: re-acknowledging an already-acknowledged
  pay app is a 200 (no-op), preserving the original
  acknowledgedAt timestamp
- 409 Conflict for PAID pay apps (you can't re-acknowledge
  after the wire has cleared)

Regression tests at app/api/pay-apps/[id]/acknowledge/
__tests__/acknowledge.test.ts cover:
  - no body
  - missing token
  - too-short token
  - token not matching any pay app
  - token matches a DIFFERENT pay app (IDOR)
  - DRAFT pay app
  - PAID pay app (409)
  - invalid email
  - valid request → update called correctly
  - idempotent re-acknowledge preserves original timestamp

================================================================
ITEM 2: HTTP security headers (next.config.mjs)
================================================================

The audit agent's main cluster of findings: only HSTS was
present, and it was missing includeSubDomains. Every
other standard header (CSP, X-Frame-Options, nosniff,
Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP/CORP) was
missing entirely. X-Powered-By was leaked.

Added a complete security header set via next.config.mjs
async headers() — applied to every route via /:path*:

  Content-Security-Policy — full policy with allowlisted
    origins for: Clerk, OSM tiles, Nominatim geocoding,
    Vercel Blob, Resend, Clerk image CDN. 'self' for
    default. frame-ancestors 'none' for clickjacking.
    object-src 'none'. 'unsafe-inline' allowed for
    script-src (Next.js streams SSR + Clerk UI needs it)
    and style-src (Tailwind injects styles).

  Strict-Transport-Security — max-age=2y, includeSubDomains,
    preload. Preload is opt-in by submitting to the HSTS
    preload list at hstspreload.org; leaving the directive
    in place doesn't auto-submit.

  X-Frame-Options: DENY — belt-and-braces fallback for
    ancient browsers that don't honor frame-ancestors.

  X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — prevent MIME sniffing.

  Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin —
    don't leak full URLs (with workspace / project IDs) to
    third-party origins.

  Permissions-Policy — allow camera=(self) and
    geolocation=(self) (we use both for Scan + GPS-tagged
    photos); deny everything else including microphone
    (we don't record audio).

  Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
  Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site
    Cross-origin isolation. Required if we ever want to
    use SharedArrayBuffer; cheap insurance today.

  X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off — minor.

  poweredByHeader: false — removed the X-Powered-By
    'Next.js' leak.

Verified with curl -I: every header present on every
response. Build still clean.

================================================================
ITEM 3: Hydration mismatch (React #425 / #422)
================================================================

Root cause: client components computed 'time-ago' strings
inline using Date.now() at render time. The server and
client produced different strings (e.g. '4 min ago' on
server, '5 min ago' on client) → React discards the server
HTML and re-renders on the client (perf hit + flicker +
console exceptions).

Fix: new <RelativeTime iso={...} /> component at
components/ui/RelativeTime.tsx that:
  - Server-renders an ABSOLUTE date (e.g. 'Aug 15') using
    a fixed en-US locale + UTC so the bytes are identical
    on server and first client render
  - On mount, useEffect swaps to the relative form
    ('4 min ago')
  - Re-renders every 30s so '5 min ago' updates while the
    user has the page open
  - Always sets title={iso.toISOString()} on the span
    for accessibility / hover
  - Falls back to 'never' for null/undefined input

Replaced inline relativeTime() calls in:
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/team/TeamPageClient.tsx
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/scan/ScanPageClient.tsx
  - app/(app)/w/[workspace]/projects/[id]/ProjectLocationBadge.tsx
  - components/messages/MessageThread.tsx
  - components/forms/DraftForm.tsx

Kept the old lib/format/relative-time.ts for the admin
pages (which are server components, no hydration issue)
and for any future server-side rendering need.

================================================================
================================================================

220 → 230 tests passing (10 new regression tests for
acknowledge). Build clean. Security headers verified via
curl -I.

That leaves two real consequences: denial of service against that one agent's queue, and
the ability to **report false findings**. Findings are data a human reads and acts on, so
treat them as untrusted input — which is the other reason nothing is auto-registered.

Revocation does not depend on reaching the container. **Revoke** clears the stored public

nearest one.

### The credential is the agent's, never the dashboard's

A dashboard connection row bound to an agent stores the agent's **name for it** and
nothing else: no host, no username, no password. The job says *"run `inventory_sync` on
`dc1-vcenter`"* and the agent resolves the rest from its own
[`connections.yaml`](../examples/remote-agent/connections.example.yaml).

That is the difference between this and a proxy. Shipping credentials in the job
envelope would put a standing vCenter administrator password in the dashboard's
database, in every job payload, in the agent's memory — and, because **envelopes are
signed rather than encrypted**, in the logs of any TLS-inspecting proxy in between. The
[whole feature is sold](#behind-a-tls-inspecting-proxy) on the opposite property.

The cost is two files joined by a string, and a typo in either yields
`unknown connection 'dc1-vcenter'`. The connection form mitigates that by offering an
agent picker rather than a free-text uuid.

### Three grants, all required

Nothing runs unless all three agree, and they belong to different people:

feat(agents): fetch hypervisor credentials just-in-time, sealed per fetch

An agent-bound hypervisor connection kept its credential on the agent host, in a
plaintext connections.yaml. Anyone who could read files there -- root, the docker
group, a backup, a copied volume -- had a standing vCenter/Proxmox administrator
password: offline, permanent, and silent, because a file read is not an event
anybody sees.

The credential can now live on the dashboard instead, and the agent fetches it for
each job over the poll channel it already has. Opt-in per connection, and the opt-in
is in the CUSTOMER's file (`dashboard_secret: true`), not a dashboard toggle -- a
credential set on the Connections page does nothing until their file says so.

This inverts a deliberate, documented trade, so the invariant is narrowed rather
than dropped: the dashboard may hold the SECRET, never the TARGET. `host` and
`username` are still always the agent's, because those aim the connection -- a
dashboard able to set `host` could redirect the agent's authenticated session at an
endpoint of its choosing and harvest the credential on first use.

With `ps_account://<id>` as the connection's secret_ref, neither side holds a
standing password: the dashboard checks one out of Password Safe per job, checks it
back in, and rotates it on release.

Sealed, not merely transported. `agent_signing` bought authentication the hard way
because an inspecting corporate proxy reads request bodies; the same proxy reads
response bodies, so the credential is encrypted at the application layer (ephemeral
X25519 -> HKDF-SHA256 -> AES-256-GCM, `services/agent_sealing`). The recipient key
is generated per fetch and rides in the already-signed request body, so there is no
new column, no enrolment change, no rotation protocol, and no decryption key on the
host to steal and use against traffic captured earlier. The AAD binds agent, job and
connection ref and is rebuilt from trusted state on both sides, never transmitted --
the ref most of all, since without it a credential can be relabelled as one for a
connection pointing somewhere else.

Notable details, each with the reason in the code:

* The connection is derived from the job row, never chosen by the request. Without
  that, a stolen agent identity enumerates every credential the dashboard holds.
* `statuses=("running",)`, not the WINDING_DOWN default: a cancelled job may still
  log and complete, but gets no fresh credential.
* The reply key is validated BEFORE the credential is obtained, so a malformed
  request cannot burn Password Safe checkouts and rotations.
* Release is ref-counted. ConflictOption=reuse hands concurrent jobs one request id,
  so releasing per job would rotate the password under a live sibling.
* The sweeper, not the completion hook, is the authority: reconcile_stale_jobs writes
  `failed` inline and never reaches complete_job, which is exactly the killed-agent
  case that matters most.
* Fetched credentials are scrubbed from everything outbound. `execute` was shipping
  raw `str(exc)[:1000]` into the job row, which is the only text a failed job renders,
  and an arbitrary library's exception message can carry a credential.
* Gated at enqueue on the agent version, so a 2.0 agent cannot fall through to a
  password the operator just deleted, send an empty one, and lock the account out.

Also fixes, in passing: `ps_api_service._checkout` left a request open when a
pending approval refused the credential, holding the account's concurrent-request
slot for the whole duration; and `update()` let an admin set `host` on an agent-bound
row, which `create()` had stripped -- harmless while nothing read it, not harmless now.

Two doc claims were already stale before this change and are corrected: "the agent
holds no target credentials" broke when hypervisor brokering shipped, and the roadmap
listed agent-side Password Safe checkout as future work when it has been live.

Tests: 67 new assertions across four files, incl. each AAD field bound independently,
the small-order key case, cross-implementation seal/open, IDOR, the shared-request
ref count, and release-on-reap. The two tests that encoded the old invariant failed
as expected and were split/extended rather than silenced.

Enforces explicit role-based access control and authority validation before executing action.

Secure customer auth with signed session tokens (fixes IDOR)

The app identified the customer with a plain x-customer-id header the client
could set to anything, so any device could read any customer's events, and a
signed-out browser saw the demo customer's data.

Now register/login issue a stateless HMAC-signed session token; the API derives
the customer strictly from that token (empty when unauthenticated, so scoped
queries return nothing rather than someone else's data). Checkout takes the
customer from the token instead of the request body. Client stores the token
and sends it as a Bearer header on every request (wallet pass included).

* .

* Phase 1 security fixes: payment auth bypass, secret hygiene, fail-closed defaults

- routes/user/payments.js: remove unauthenticated duplicate payment
  routes. Express's default (non-strict) router already matches both
  trailing-slash variants on the single protected handler, so the
  "aliases" only existed to create an unauthenticated payment path.
- controllers/user/paymentController.js (verifyPayment): stop trusting
  client-supplied `amount` — always re-derive platformFee/vendorAmount
  from Booking -> Service.price. Require a real Razorpay signature for
  online gateways; for cash-like methods, require the booking to
  belong to the authenticated user instead of skipping verification
  outright.
- validators/user/paymentValidators.js: bookingId now required on
  verify (needed to look up the authoritative price); amount removed
  from the accepted body since it's no longer read.
- util/cors.js, middleware/errorMiddleware.js: flip permissive-by-
  default checks (`!== 'production'`) to explicit opt-in
  (`=== 'development'`), so an unset/misconfigured NODE_ENV fails
  closed (strict CORS, no stack traces) instead of failing open.
- controllers/authController.js: sign refresh tokens with
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET instead of the access-token secret; rotate the
  refresh token (and blacklist the old one via Redis) on every use
  instead of re-issuing the same one indefinitely. Stop leaking
  error.message from the phone-OTP send endpoint.
- routes/auth.js: apply strictAuthLimiter to the four password-reset
  endpoints (forgot-password, send-password-reset-otp,
  reset-password-otp, reset-password/:uid/:token), matching the limiter
  already applied to signup/login/OTP-send.
- middleware/authMiddleware.js: export isRefreshTokenBlacklisted for
  use by the rotation logic above.

* Phase 2: DB indexes, real health check, financial-record protection

All schema changes applied additively via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY /
ALTER TABLE against the live Supabase DB directly (prisma db push
can't reach it through the pgbouncer pooler used here) — no drops, no
data loss. Two real schema/DB drifts were also found and fixed along
the way (see below).

Indexes added (were causing full table scans on frequently-filtered
columns): Payment.status, Payment.vendorPayoutStatus,
VendorProfile.city/status/is_online, Review.vendorId,
Document/Inventory/Availability/Promotion.vendorId, Feedback.userId,
EmailOTP.email.

Schema drift fixed while adding the Review.vendorId index: the live
DB's Review table had no vendorId column at all, despite schema.prisma
defining it and reviewController.js/serviceConfirmationController.js
(from the Phase 0 merge) reading it directly. Added the column,
backfilled all 8 existing rows from Booking->Service.vendorId, and
added the matching FK + index.

Second drift found while changing onDelete rules: PayoutSettlement
didn't exist as a table on the live DB at all, even though the
async payout-worker code kept in Phase 0 depends on it. Created it to
match schema.prisma exactly.

- prisma/schema.prisma, server.js, controllers/Admin/userController.js:
  Booking.user and Payment.booking changed from onDelete: Cascade to
  Restrict, so deleting a User can no longer silently cascade-delete
  their Booking/Payment/PayoutSettlement financial trail.
  controllers/Admin/userController.js's deleteUser now soft-deletes
  (is_active = false) users with any booking history instead of
  hard-deleting, since a hard delete would now correctly fail against
  the new constraint.
- server.js: /health now actually pings Postgres and Redis (each with
  a 2s timeout so an unreachable dependency can't hang the response)
  instead of just checking that the client objects were constructed.
  Also wires up the new OTP cleanup worker/queue and its graceful
  shutdown.
- queues/otpCleanupQueue.js, workers/otpCleanupWorker.js: hourly BullMQ
  repeatable job pruning expired EmailOTP rows (and verified ones past
  a 24h retention window) — previously only pruned on next-OTP-request
  for the same address, so rows for addresses that never request
  another OTP accumulated forever.
- db.js, "postgres" dependency: removed — a second, entirely unused
  raw connection pool alongside the real Prisma-managed one.
- package.json: removed @prisma/adapter-ppg, an unused duplicate of
  @prisma/adapter-pg (the one actually in use).

* Extract payment/payout/booking-confirmation business logic into services/

Controllers previously mixed HTTP concerns (parsing req, shaping res)
with the actual business logic and Prisma transactions directly,
which is why the payment-amount bug from Phase 1 was sitting in a
controller in the first place. Each extracted service throws a typed
Error subclass carrying an intended HTTP status code; the controller's
catch block maps it to a response, so the service layer has no
knowledge of Express and is unit-testable on its own.

- services/paymentService.js (verifyAndRecordPayment, PaymentError):
  extracted from paymentController.js's verifyPayment — signature
  verification, cash-like-gateway ownership check, fee calculation,
  and the payment+booking transaction.
- services/payoutService.js (claimAndQueuePayout, PayoutError):
  extracted from financeController.js's settlePayout — the
  claim-then-queue transaction for the admin-triggered async payout
  flow (BullMQ payoutQueue/payoutWorker).
- services/bookingConfirmationService.js (confirmBookingAndQueuePayout,
  BookingConfirmationError): extracted from
  serviceConfirmationController.js's confirmServiceCompletion — the
  booking-confirm + optional-review + payout-claim transaction. Also
  removed an unused createNotification import left over from an
  earlier merge.
- services/vendorPayoutService.js (triggerVendorPayoutNow,
  VendorPayoutError): extracted from vendorPayoutController.js's
  triggerVendorPayout — the synchronous (non-queued) admin payout path
  that requires an active VendorPayoutAccount. Also removed a
  never-used Razorpay client instance left over from an earlier merge.

These three payout-adjacent flows (queued via payoutService, inline
via vendorPayoutService, and the booking-confirmation trigger) remain
intentionally separate rather than merged into one — they have
genuinely different preconditions and gateway-call semantics, and
consolidating them is a bigger design decision than today's mechanical
extraction.

* .

* Phase 1 security fixes: payment auth bypass, secret hygiene, fail-closed defaults

- routes/user/payments.js: remove unauthenticated duplicate payment
  routes. Express's default (non-strict) router already matches both
  trailing-slash variants on the single protected handler, so the
  "aliases" only existed to create an unauthenticated payment path.
- controllers/user/paymentController.js (verifyPayment): stop trusting
  client-supplied `amount` — always re-derive platformFee/vendorAmount
  from Booking -> Service.price. Require a real Razorpay signature for
  online gateways; for cash-like methods, require the booking to
  belong to the authenticated user instead of skipping verification
  outright.
- validators/user/paymentValidators.js: bookingId now required on
  verify (needed to look up the authoritative price); amount removed
  from the accepted body since it's no longer read.
- util/cors.js, middleware/errorMiddleware.js: flip permissive-by-
  default checks (`!== 'production'`) to explicit opt-in
  (`=== 'development'`), so an unset/misconfigured NODE_ENV fails
  closed (strict CORS, no stack traces) instead of failing open.
- controllers/authController.js: sign refresh tokens with
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET instead of the access-token secret; rotate the
  refresh token (and blacklist the old one via Redis) on every use
  instead of re-issuing the same one indefinitely. Stop leaking
  error.message from the phone-OTP send endpoint.
- routes/auth.js: apply strictAuthLimiter to the four password-reset
  endpoints (forgot-password, send-password-reset-otp,
  reset-password-otp, reset-password/:uid/:token), matching the limiter
  already applied to signup/login/OTP-send.
- middleware/authMiddleware.js: export isRefreshTokenBlacklisted for
  use by the rotation logic above.

* Phase 2: DB indexes, real health check, financial-record protection

All schema changes applied additively via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY /
ALTER TABLE against the live Supabase DB directly (prisma db push
can't reach it through the pgbouncer pooler used here) — no drops, no
data loss. Two real schema/DB drifts were also found and fixed along
the way (see below).

Indexes added (were causing full table scans on frequently-filtered
columns): Payment.status, Payment.vendorPayoutStatus,
VendorProfile.city/status/is_online, Review.vendorId,
Document/Inventory/Availability/Promotion.vendorId, Feedback.userId,
EmailOTP.email.

Schema drift fixed while adding the Review.vendorId index: the live
DB's Review table had no vendorId column at all, despite schema.prisma
defining it and reviewController.js/serviceConfirmationController.js
(from the Phase 0 merge) reading it directly. Added the column,
backfilled all 8 existing rows from Booking->Service.vendorId, and
added the matching FK + index.

Second drift found while changing onDelete rules: PayoutSettlement
didn't exist as a table on the live DB at all, even though the
async payout-worker code kept in Phase 0 depends on it. Created it to
match schema.prisma exactly.

- prisma/schema.prisma, server.js, controllers/Admin/userController.js:
  Booking.user and Payment.booking changed from onDelete: Cascade to
  Restrict, so deleting a User can no longer silently cascade-delete
  their Booking/Payment/PayoutSettlement financial trail.
  controllers/Admin/userController.js's deleteUser now soft-deletes
  (is_active = false) users with any booking history instead of
  hard-deleting, since a hard delete would now correctly fail against
  the new constraint.
- server.js: /health now actually pings Postgres and Redis (each with
  a 2s timeout so an unreachable dependency can't hang the response)
  instead of just checking that the client objects were constructed.
  Also wires up the new OTP cleanup worker/queue and its graceful
  shutdown.
- queues/otpCleanupQueue.js, workers/otpCleanupWorker.js: hourly BullMQ
  repeatable job pruning expired EmailOTP rows (and verified ones past
  a 24h retention window) — previously only pruned on next-OTP-request
  for the same address, so rows for addresses that never request
  another OTP accumulated forever.
- db.js, "postgres" dependency: removed — a second, entirely unused
  raw connection pool alongside the real Prisma-managed one.
- package.json: removed @prisma/adapter-ppg, an unused duplicate of
  @prisma/adapter-pg (the one actually in use).

* Extract payment/payout/booking-confirmation business logic into services/

Controllers previously mixed HTTP concerns (parsing req, shaping res)
with the actual business logic and Prisma transactions directly,
which is why the payment-amount bug from Phase 1 was sitting in a
controller in the first place. Each extracted service throws a typed
Error subclass carrying an intended HTTP status code; the controller's
catch block maps it to a response, so the service layer has no
knowledge of Express and is unit-testable on its own.

- services/paymentService.js (verifyAndRecordPayment, PaymentError):
  extracted from paymentController.js's verifyPayment — signature
  verification, cash-like-gateway ownership check, fee calculation,
  and the payment+booking transaction.
- services/payoutService.js (claimAndQueuePayout, PayoutError):
  extracted from financeController.js's settlePayout — the
  claim-then-queue transaction for the admin-triggered async payout
  flow (BullMQ payoutQueue/payoutWorker).
- services/bookingConfirmationService.js (confirmBookingAndQueuePayout,
  BookingConfirmationError): extracted from
  serviceConfirmationController.js's confirmServiceCompletion — the
  booking-confirm + optional-review + payout-claim transaction. Also
  removed an unused createNotification import left over from an
  earlier merge.
- services/vendorPayoutService.js (triggerVendorPayoutNow,
  VendorPayoutError): extracted from vendorPayoutController.js's
  triggerVendorPayout — the synchronous (non-queued) admin payout path
  that requires an active VendorPayoutAccount. Also removed a
  never-used Razorpay client instance left over from an earlier merge.

These three payout-adjacent flows (queued via payoutService, inline
via vendorPayoutService, and the booking-confirmation trigger) remain
intentionally separate rather than merged into one — they have
genuinely different preconditions and gateway-call semantics, and
consolidating them is a bigger design decision than today's mechanical
extraction.

* .

* Phase 1 security fixes: payment auth bypass, secret hygiene, fail-closed defaults

- routes/user/payments.js: remove unauthenticated duplicate payment
  routes. Express's default (non-strict) router already matches both
  trailing-slash variants on the single protected handler, so the
  "aliases" only existed to create an unauthenticated payment path.
- controllers/user/paymentController.js (verifyPayment): stop trusting
  client-supplied `amount` — always re-derive platformFee/vendorAmount
  from Booking -> Service.price. Require a real Razorpay signature for
  online gateways; for cash-like methods, require the booking to
  belong to the authenticated user instead of skipping verification
  outright.
- validators/user/paymentValidators.js: bookingId now required on
  verify (needed to look up the authoritative price); amount removed
  from the accepted body since it's no longer read.
- util/cors.js, middleware/errorMiddleware.js: flip permissive-by-
  default checks (`!== 'production'`) to explicit opt-in
  (`=== 'development'`), so an unset/misconfigured NODE_ENV fails
  closed (strict CORS, no stack traces) instead of failing open.
- controllers/authController.js: sign refresh tokens with
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET instead of the access-token secret; rotate the
  refresh token (and blacklist the old one via Redis) on every use
  instead of re-issuing the same one indefinitely. Stop leaking
  error.message from the phone-OTP send endpoint.
- routes/auth.js: apply strictAuthLimiter to the four password-reset
  endpoints (forgot-password, send-password-reset-otp,
  reset-password-otp, reset-password/:uid/:token), matching the limiter
  already applied to signup/login/OTP-send.
- middleware/authMiddleware.js: export isRefreshTokenBlacklisted for
  use by the rotation logic above.

* Phase 2: DB indexes, real health check, financial-record protection

All schema changes applied additively via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY /
ALTER TABLE against the live Supabase DB directly (prisma db push
can't reach it through the pgbouncer pooler used here) — no drops, no
data loss. Two real schema/DB drifts were also found and fixed along
the way (see below).

Indexes added (were causing full table scans on frequently-filtered
columns): Payment.status, Payment.vendorPayoutStatus,
VendorProfile.city/status/is_online, Review.vendorId,
Document/Inventory/Availability/Promotion.vendorId, Feedback.userId,
EmailOTP.email.

Schema drift fixed while adding the Review.vendorId index: the live
DB's Review table had no vendorId column at all, despite schema.prisma
defining it and reviewController.js/serviceConfirmationController.js
(from the Phase 0 merge) reading it directly. Added the column,
backfilled all 8 existing rows from Booking->Service.vendorId, and
added the matching FK + index.

Second drift found while changing onDelete rules: PayoutSettlement
didn't exist as a table on the live DB at all, even though the
async payout-worker code kept in Phase 0 depends on it. Created it to
match schema.prisma exactly.

- prisma/schema.prisma, server.js, controllers/Admin/userController.js:
  Booking.user and Payment.booking changed from onDelete: Cascade to
  Restrict, so deleting a User can no longer silently cascade-delete
  their Booking/Payment/PayoutSettlement financial trail.
  controllers/Admin/userController.js's deleteUser now soft-deletes
  (is_active = false) users with any booking history instead of
  hard-deleting, since a hard delete would now correctly fail against
  the new constraint.
- server.js: /health now actually pings Postgres and Redis (each with
  a 2s timeout so an unreachable dependency can't hang the response)
  instead of just checking that the client objects were constructed.
  Also wires up the new OTP cleanup worker/queue and its graceful
  shutdown.
- queues/otpCleanupQueue.js, workers/otpCleanupWorker.js: hourly BullMQ
  repeatable job pruning expired EmailOTP rows (and verified ones past
  a 24h retention window) — previously only pruned on next-OTP-request
  for the same address, so rows for addresses that never request
  another OTP accumulated forever.
- db.js, "postgres" dependency: removed — a second, entirely unused
  raw connection pool alongside the real Prisma-managed one.
- package.json: removed @prisma/adapter-ppg, an unused duplicate of
  @prisma/adapter-pg (the one actually in use).

* Extract payment/payout/booking-confirmation business logic into services/

Controllers previously mixed HTTP concerns (parsing req, shaping res)
with the actual business logic and Prisma transactions directly,
which is why the payment-amount bug from Phase 1 was sitting in a
controller in the first place. Each extracted service throws a typed
Error subclass carrying an intended HTTP status code; the controller's
catch block maps it to a response, so the service layer has no
knowledge of Express and is unit-testable on its own.

- services/paymentService.js (verifyAndRecordPayment, PaymentError):
  extracted from paymentController.js's verifyPayment — signature
  verification, cash-like-gateway ownership check, fee calculation,
  and the payment+booking transaction.
- services/payoutService.js (claimAndQueuePayout, PayoutError):
  extracted from financeController.js's settlePayout — the
  claim-then-queue transaction for the admin-triggered async payout
  flow (BullMQ payoutQueue/payoutWorker).
- services/bookingConfirmationService.js (confirmBookingAndQueuePayout,
  BookingConfirmationError): extracted from
  serviceConfirmationController.js's confirmServiceCompletion — the
  booking-confirm + optional-review + payout-claim transaction. Also
  removed an unused createNotification import left over from an
  earlier merge.
- services/vendorPayoutService.js (triggerVendorPayoutNow,
  VendorPayoutError): extracted from vendorPayoutController.js's
  triggerVendorPayout — the synchronous (non-queued) admin payout path
  that requires an active VendorPayoutAccount. Also removed a
  never-used Razorpay client instance left over from an earlier merge.

These three payout-adjacent flows (queued via payoutService, inline
via vendorPayoutService, and the booking-confirmation trigger) remain
intentionally separate rather than merged into one — they have
genuinely different preconditions and gateway-call semantics, and
consolidating them is a bigger design decision than today's mechanical
extraction.

* .

* Phase 1 security fixes: payment auth bypass, secret hygiene, fail-closed defaults

- routes/user/payments.js: remove unauthenticated duplicate payment
  routes. Express's default (non-strict) router already matches both
  trailing-slash variants on the single protected handler, so the
  "aliases" only existed to create an unauthenticated payment path.
- controllers/user/paymentController.js (verifyPayment): stop trusting
  client-supplied `amount` — always re-derive platformFee/vendorAmount
  from Booking -> Service.price. Require a real Razorpay signature for
  online gateways; for cash-like methods, require the booking to
  belong to the authenticated user instead of skipping verification
  outright.
- validators/user/paymentValidators.js: bookingId now required on
  verify (needed to look up the authoritative price); amount removed
  from the accepted body since it's no longer read.
- util/cors.js, middleware/errorMiddleware.js: flip permissive-by-
  default checks (`!== 'production'`) to explicit opt-in
  (`=== 'development'`), so an unset/misconfigured NODE_ENV fails
  closed (strict CORS, no stack traces) instead of failing open.
- controllers/authController.js: sign refresh tokens with
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET instead of the access-token secret; rotate the
  refresh token (and blacklist the old one via Redis) on every use
  instead of re-issuing the same one indefinitely. Stop leaking
  error.message from the phone-OTP send endpoint.
- routes/auth.js: apply strictAuthLimiter to the four password-reset
  endpoints (forgot-password, send-password-reset-otp,
  reset-password-otp, reset-password/:uid/:token), matching the limiter
  already applied to signup/login/OTP-send.
- middleware/authMiddleware.js: export isRefreshTokenBlacklisted for
  use by the rotation logic above.

* Phase 2: DB indexes, real health check, financial-record protection

All schema changes applied additively via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY /
ALTER TABLE against the live Supabase DB directly (prisma db push
can't reach it through the pgbouncer pooler used here) — no drops, no
data loss. Two real schema/DB drifts were also found and fixed along
the way (see below).

Indexes added (were causing full table scans on frequently-filtered
columns): Payment.status, Payment.vendorPayoutStatus,
VendorProfile.city/status/is_online, Review.vendorId,
Document/Inventory/Availability/Promotion.vendorId, Feedback.userId,
EmailOTP.email.

Schema drift fixed while adding the Review.vendorId index: the live
DB's Review table had no vendorId column at all, despite schema.prisma
defining it and reviewController.js/serviceConfirmationController.js
(from the Phase 0 merge) reading it directly. Added the column,
backfilled all 8 existing rows from Booking->Service.vendorId, and
added the matching FK + index.

Second drift found while changing onDelete rules: PayoutSettlement
didn't exist as a table on the live DB at all, even though the
async payout-worker code kept in Phase 0 depends on it. Created it to
match schema.prisma exactly.

- prisma/schema.prisma, server.js, controllers/Admin/userController.js:
  Booking.user and Payment.booking changed from onDelete: Cascade to
  Restrict, so deleting a User can no longer silently cascade-delete
  their Booking/Payment/PayoutSettlement financial trail.
  controllers/Admin/userController.js's deleteUser now soft-deletes
  (is_active = false) users with any booking history instead of
  hard-deleting, since a hard delete would now correctly fail against
  the new constraint.
- server.js: /health now actually pings Postgres and Redis (each with
  a 2s timeout so an unreachable dependency can't hang the response)
  instead of just checking that the client objects were constructed.
  Also wires up the new OTP cleanup worker/queue and its graceful
  shutdown.
- queues/otpCleanupQueue.js, workers/otpCleanupWorker.js: hourly BullMQ
  repeatable job pruning expired EmailOTP rows (and verified ones past
  a 24h retention window) — previously only pruned on next-OTP-request
  for the same address, so rows for addresses that never request
  another OTP accumulated forever.
- db.js, "postgres" dependency: removed — a second, entirely unused
  raw connection pool alongside the real Prisma-managed one.
- package.json: removed @prisma/adapter-ppg, an unused duplicate of
  @prisma/adapter-pg (the one actually in use).

* Extract payment/payout/booking-confirmation business logic into services/

Controllers previously mixed HTTP concerns (parsing req, shaping res)
with the actual business logic and Prisma transactions directly,
which is why the payment-amount bug from Phase 1 was sitting in a
controller in the first place. Each extracted service throws a typed
Error subclass carrying an intended HTTP status code; the controller's
catch block maps it to a response, so the service layer has no
knowledge of Express and is unit-testable on its own.

- services/paymentService.js (verifyAndRecordPayment, PaymentError):
  extracted from paymentController.js's verifyPayment — signature
  verification, cash-like-gateway ownership check, fee calculation,
  and the payment+booking transaction.
- services/payoutService.js (claimAndQueuePayout, PayoutError):
  extracted from financeController.js's settlePayout — the
  claim-then-queue transaction for the admin-triggered async payout
  flow (BullMQ payoutQueue/payoutWorker).
- services/bookingConfirmationService.js (confirmBookingAndQueuePayout,
  BookingConfirmationError): extracted from
  serviceConfirmationController.js's confirmServiceCompletion — the
  booking-confirm + optional-review + payout-claim transaction. Also
  removed an unused createNotification import left over from an
  earlier merge.
- services/vendorPayoutService.js (triggerVendorPayoutNow,
  VendorPayoutError): extracted from vendorPayoutController.js's
  triggerVendorPayout — the synchronous (non-queued) admin payout path
  that requires an active VendorPayoutAccount. Also removed a
  never-used Razorpay client instance left over from an earlier merge.

These three payout-adjacent flows (queued via payoutService, inline
via vendorPayoutService, and the booking-confirmation trigger) remain
intentionally separate rather than merged into one — they have
genuinely different preconditions and gateway-call semantics, and
consolidating them is a bigger design decision than today's mechanical
extraction.

fix(cli): repair the REST transport — branch add, user management, board export/clone/import (#2476)

* fix(cli): authenticate custom-method REST calls

The Feathers authentication hook decorates the standard service methods but
not custom methods registered via `service.methods(...)`, so every CLI call to
one went out with no Authorization header and the daemon answered 401
"Not authenticated". That covered `agor board export`, `board clone` and
`board import`.

Only the CLI was affected: the UI talks Socket.IO, where the connection itself
is authenticated, so nothing in the product exercised this path.

Attach the bearer at the transport layer instead, so standard and custom
methods are covered alike with no per-method wiring to forget. The token is
tracked as it is established rather than read back from the authentication
client, which is configured with `storage: undefined` and therefore resolves
`getAccessToken()` to null. The login exchange is explicitly excluded so a
stale token cannot 401 the very call meant to replace it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): authenticate /users requests over REST

`agor user list`, `user create`, `user update` and `user delete` all failed
with 401 "Authentication required" against a valid superadmin token, while
every other service accepted the same token. The whole command group was
unusable.

The users service cannot take a blanket `requireAuth` the way other services
do, because it deliberately serves two unauthenticated callers: internal calls
with no `provider`, and the Feathers local-auth email lookup during login. It
had no authenticate hook at all as a result, so `params.user` was never
populated on the REST transport and every downstream guard that reads it — the
`find` hook, `authorizeUsersGet`, the role checks — rejected the request.

Socket.IO connections carry `params.user` from the authenticated connection,
which is why the UI was unaffected and this only ever showed up in the CLI.

Authenticate when the caller actually presented credentials, leaving both
intentional unauthenticated paths untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): enforce password change after authentication, not before

A user flagged `must_change_password` could do anything the CLI offered. The
gate held over Socket.IO but passed everything through over REST, so a
bootstrap admin created with a temporary password could keep using it
indefinitely.

The cause is hook ordering rather than transport. `enforcePasswordChange` is
registered as a global `app.hooks({before: {all: [...]}})`, and Feathers runs
app-level hooks *before* service-level ones — so it fired while the service's
own `requireAuth` had not yet populated `params.user`, hit its
`if (!user) return context` guard, and let the call through. Socket.IO
connections already carry `params.user` when the app hook runs, which is why
the gate worked there.

Run the check at the auth chokepoint, immediately after authentication
resolves, so the user is actually populated. The global hook stays in place and
still covers calls that arrive already authenticated.

Verified: 403 while flagged, 200 once cleared, and `agor login` itself is
unaffected in both states.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): create branches through the /repos/:id/branches route

`agor branch add` — the core "isolated branch" workflow — could never succeed.
It threw a raw `client.service(...).createBranch is not a function` at the user
after already doing the git work.

`RepoService.createBranch()` takes `(id, data)`, which is not the Feathers
custom-method contract, and it is not in the `/repos` transport method list, so
it is unreachable over REST and silently unanswered over Socket.IO. Listing it
is not the fix: the signature would still not match, and two in-process callers
depend on it as-is.

Branch creation is already exposed as the RBAC-guarded `/repos/:id/branches`
route, which is what the UI uses. Point the CLI at the same route rather than
adding a second path to the same operation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): make daemon start non-interactive, move deployment-id repair to doctor

Starting a daemon is what service managers, containers and provisioning scripts
do, so `agor daemon start` must not block on a prompt and must not rewrite
config.yaml as a side effect. A missing `daemon.deployment_id` did both: on a
TTY it dropped into an inquirer confirm offering to rewrite the file.

`daemon start` now fails hard and points at `agor doctor`, which owns the
interactive repair and reports the same state in `--json`. A generic wrapper
adds the doctor pointer to any other startup failure, suppressed when the
message already names its own remedy.

The repair also stops assuming a fresh ID is wanted. It offers a generated one
but accepts a pasted value, and the error text says plainly that a new ID
re-identifies the deployment and forces every connected client to log in again.
Recovering a deployment's previous identity was impossible before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): scope init's running-daemon guard to this deployment

`agor init` refused to run whenever *any* daemon answered on the configured
URL, and for a home with no config yet that URL is the global default. So
initializing a brand-new home failed because an unrelated deployment happened
to occupy port 3030, and `--daemon-port` could not get around it since the
guard probed before the flag was applied.

The same false positive made the `agor init` test suite depend on no daemon
running locally: eight tests failed on a developer machine with a live daemon
and passed only in CI.

Consider only daemons this home actually owns — one it manages via its PID
file, or one answering on its configured URL whose deployment ID matches. A
port is not ownership.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): keep doctor ok on an uninitialized install

Reporting the deployment ID in doctor also folded it into `ok`, which broke the
packaged-install smoke test: it runs `agor doctor --json` against a freshly
installed, never-initialized Agor and asserts `ok` is true.

A fresh install legitimately has no config.yaml and therefore no deployment ID —
that is what `agor init` is for, not a fault. Only a config that exists and is
missing the ID is a real problem, because that is the case where `daemon start`
refuses.

Scope the check to an initialized installation, report `initialized` alongside
`present` so the two states are distinguishable, and say "Not initialized yet"
in the text output rather than showing a red failure on a healthy new install.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ui): fix racy chip assertions in AgenticConfigChipRow

Both cases wait for the "Custom" source label to appear and then immediately
assert that a *different* element — the model or effort chip — has already
re-rendered. Those are separate effects of one state change, so on a loaded CI
runner the chip can still hold its previous text; the effort case failed with
"Effort: Inherited" where "Effort: Medium" was expected.

Wrap the chip assertions in their own waitFor. Unrelated to the rest of this
branch, but it was the only thing failing CI.

on a beta deployment where launching from a different directory than

previously-registered users disappear ("user not found").

resolve against the executable's directory like everything else in

fix(ci): a rotated BYOD token must announce a skip, not red the deploy

The BYOD smoke suite runs against a third-party Supabase project named only by
two secrets — a project this pipeline never deploys to. `deploy.yml` documents
it as opt-in coverage whose contract is "an absent configuration self-skips" and
"only a real BYOD assertion failure fails the step", but a token that project no
longer accepts was neither, and it failed the step: every BYOD test errors with
MCP -32001, reddening smoke-preview and, through the lockstep gate, blocking the
production deploy of an unrelated change (run 32217158749, failing since
2026-08-18 19:13Z).

Probe the credential once before the suite is collected and widen exactly one
outcome into an announced skip: JSON-RPC -32001. That code is emitted in one
place (the edge's missing/invalid/rotated-token branch) and mcp-authz-status
already pins that every authorization denial uses JSONRPC_FORBIDDEN instead, so
it cannot mean anything but "this project does not accept this token". Every
other outcome — an HTTP error, an unreachable host, a 5xx, a wrong answer — still
fails the suite, so no regression in the memory tools can hide behind it.

The skip is loud (console + a ::warning:: annotation naming the rotation) so
lost coverage is visible rather than silent, and two drift guards pin that the
escape hatch stays narrow.
Validates cryptographic signature and claims on the authentication token before granting access.

fix(api): include component in exec authorization hierarchy (#4506)

Motivation:
When a role binding's scope is restricted to a specific component,
the bound role could not exec into that component, even though the
binding explicitly granted access to it. ExecHandler.ServeHTTP built
the authz.ResourceHierarchy for the component:exec permission check
with only Namespace and Project set, omitting Component, even though
the component name was already known at that point in the handler.

The Casbin policy matcher (resourceMatch in
internal/authz/casbin/helpers.go) only allows a policy path to match
a request path when the policy path is an exact match or a strict
prefix of it. Because the exec request's hierarchy path omitted the
component/<name> segment, a component-scoped policy's path (which
includes that segment) could never be a prefix of, or equal to, the
shorter request path, so it could never match and exec was denied.
Namespace- and project-scoped bindings were unaffected because their
shorter policy path remained a valid prefix of the request path.

Approach:
Set Component: componentName in the authz.ResourceHierarchy literal
built by ExecHandler.ServeHTTP, matching the convention already used
by every other component-scoped authorization check in the codebase
(e.g. service_authz.go, wirelogs.go). Updated the existing unit test
that previously encoded the buggy (missing-Component) hierarchy as
its expected value.

Validation:
Confirmed with a targeted unit test. Before the fix,
`go test ./internal/openchoreo-api/api/handlers/... -run TestExecHandler_AuthzEnvironmentContext_ExplicitEnv`
fails with a hierarchy mismatch (Component empty instead of
"greeter-service"); after the fix, it passes. Also ran
`go build ./...`, `go test ./internal/openchoreo-api/... ./internal/authz/...`
(all pass), and `make lint` (0 issues) locally. Did not run a live
cluster / e2e exec reproduction; the defect and fix are fully
provable at the unit-test level since the Casbin policy-path matcher
is exercised directly by the handler's authz check request, with no
live-cluster dependency.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail on ruff violations in changed Python files only."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections.abc import Sequence
from pathlib import Path

EXIT_OK = 0
EXIT_VIOLATIONS = 1
EXIT_CONFIG = 2

def git_diff_name_only(base_ref: str, repo_root: Path) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
    return subprocess.run(
        [
            "git",
            "-C",
            str(repo_root),
            "diff",
            "--name-only",
            "--diff-filter=ACMR",
            f"{base_ref}...HEAD",
        ],

)

def changed_python_files(base_ref: str, repo_root: Path) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    result = git_diff_name_only(base_ref, repo_root)
    if result.returncode != 0 and base_ref != _FALLBACK_BASE_REF:
        result = git_diff_name_only(_FALLBACK_BASE_REF, repo_root)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        print(result.stderr.strip(), file=sys.stderr)
        return EXIT_EXTERNAL, []

    files = [
        line
        for line in result.stdout.splitlines()
        if line.endswith(".py") and (repo_root / line).is_file()
    ]
    return EXIT_OK, files

def run_ruff(files: Sequence[str], repo_root: Path) -> int:
    if not files:
        print("No changed Python files found. Ruff ratchet passed.")
        return EXIT_OK

    result = subprocess.run(
        ["ruff", "check", "--output-format=github", "--", *files],
        check=False,
        capture_output=True,
        cwd=repo_root,
        text=True,
        errors="replace",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    if result.stdout:
        print(result.stdout, end="")
    if result.stderr:
        print(result.stderr, file=sys.stderr, end="")

    if result.returncode == 0:
        print(f"Ruff ratchet passed for {len(files)} changed Python file(s).")
        return EXIT_OK
    if result.returncode == 1:
        print(f"Ruff ratchet failed for {len(files)} changed Python file(s).", file=sys.stderr)

## Independent review

Run through this repo's `code-review` skill at high effort against the
branch diff. Seven findings; four were fail-open defects in my own first
two commits. All fixed in commit 3, each with a regression test that
fails on the pre-fix code:

1. **Quoted `b/` prefix.** Git C-quotes the prefix and path as one unit,
so `(?:b/)?` in the header pattern could not strip it, and the map key
became `b/od"d.py` while ruff reported `od"d.py`. Every finding in such
a file read as pre-existing. Fixed: unquote first, then strip.
Regression test drives a real git repo.
2. **Pathspec defeated rename detection.** `git diff ... -- ` drops the
delete half of the rename pair, so a pure rename came back as a
full-file add and every latent finding blocked. Fixed: no pathspec,
filter the parsed map. Regression test does a real `git mv`.
3. **Stale base ref not propagated.** `main` built the line map from the
requested ref even when the file list came from the `origin/main`
fallback; the map dropped to `None` and the gate blocked on everything.
Fixed: `changed_python_files` returns the ref that resolved.
4. **Unrelativizable path failed open.** A ruff filename outside the
repo root fell back to the absolute path, which can never match the map.
Fixed: it blocks.

Also applied: defensive row reads (ruff already emits a null `row` on
some diagnostics, and an exception out of `main` is indistinguishable
from a lint failure at the exit code), and two docstring claims
corrected.

The three findings not counted as defects were documentation accuracy
items folded into the same commit.

### A fifth defect the pre-push gate caught (commit 4)

Fixing defect 1 meant the shared header pattern had to stop stripping
`b/`, since git quotes the prefix and the path as one unit.
`git_hook_policy._iter_diff_changes` was a third consumer of that
pattern and still stripped the prefix itself, so it began reporting
every path as `b/pkg/a.py`. The **security-suppression scanner**
compares those paths against the pushed set, so a net-new `# noqa: S` /
`# nosec` / `# type: ignore` stopped matching and the gate passed it.
That is a fail-open in a security gate, caused by my own refactor.

Pre-push caught it: 14 tests in `tests/test_lefthook_integration.py`
went red and **blocked the push**. Commit `d0de2ef84` routes the header
through `_file_header_path` (unquote, then strip, `None` for a
`/dev/null` post-image) and adds three tests. The two
`_iter_diff_changes` tests were verified to fail on the pre-fix code by
reverting the fix and re-running.

Worth noting for the reviewer: the gate under change is what caught the
bug in the change. That is the intended behavior, and it is the reason
this PR is five commits rather than three.

Commit `ffa396c2b` is the last one: `list.append` returns `None`, so a
`seen.append(x) or {}` stub inside a lambda tripped mypy's
`func-returns-value` and the pre-push Mypy Changed Files ratchet blocked
the push a second time. Replaced with a named function. My verification
gap was running mypy on the two production scripts but not on the test
files; the ratchet checks every changed file. All eight touched files
now type-check together.

## Multi-agent delegation

`delegatesTo` declares which other agents an agent may hand work to. 0.18.2: a floor that isn't load-bearing, and re-draft advice that was ours to correct

Adopts just-dna-enricher 0.6.4 — a fourth partial cut, format and compiler
unchanged at 0.6.1. No sweep, no migration, no schema move. Also adopts ruff
as the project linter and applies it.

0.6.4 is the first enricher floor in pyproject.toml that is NOT hard, and the
pin says so. Every one above it was forced by something concrete: a symbol
that did not exist, a subclass whose meaning changed, an argument that went
from inert to live. This one is a single fix inside upstream's
clinvar_draft.py, in the ClinVar drafter — authoring-side code this service
does not have and never calls. A deployment left on 0.6.3 loses nothing. It
moves for assembly rather than function: the lock had already resolved 0.6.4
under the >=0.6.3 constraint, and the suite gating this release ran on
exactly 0.6.1/0.6.1/0.6.4, so a floor left behind would permit a trio nobody
tested while shipping a lock for one we did. Recorded as soft because the
long 0.6.2 and 0.6.3 arguments stop working if every floor reads mandatory.

The part that matters is a correction to advice this project published.
0.18.1 relayed upstream's remediation as "those modules need a fresh upload
from their publisher". Upstream 0.6.4 (S45) measured the half the 0.6.3 note
explicitly did not claim to have measured. The two 0.6.3 drafting fixes
remediate differently: S44 skipped rows, so a re-draft recovers them exactly
and needs no caveat. S41 wrote rows under an identity that has since moved,
and drafting appends rather than mutates — so re-running the fixed drafter
over the same spec adds the coordinate-keyed rows beside the collapsed
rsid-only row they replace. On MLH1 at min_review_stars=2, a stale module of
996 rows re-drafts to 1,061 against a fresh draft's 1,030: nothing missing,
but 31 rows a fresh draft does not contain, the leftover bearing the
mislabelled expansion. Following the shorter instruction leaves a module
worse-formed than either the old one or a new one. The remediation to pass to
a publisher is a fresh spec directory reconciled against the old module, and
UPGRADE.md now says that.

There is no registry-side detector to build, recorded before someone tries.
A coordinate-identity row carries no rsid, so the obvious predicate — an
rsid-only row whose rsID also appears on a coordinate row — finds 0 of the
31. Only the running pass can identify them, because only it holds the set of
rsIDs it is writing by coordinate that run. A facet, a revalidate rule or an
upgrade gap test would each report clean on an affected module.

ruff config mirrors just-dna-format's rather than being invented here; the
three local differences (.claude excluded, tests/* rooted, FastAPI defaults
folded into the B008 exemption) are recorded in the block. 403 findings to
zero across 54 files, mostly mechanical. Three that were not: SIM118 would
have introduced a bug, since catalog rows are sqlite3.Row whose __contains__
scans values rather than keys — the rewrite silently switches off featured,
needs_upgrade, downloads and the signed check. A shadowed
namespaces_for_account, live since 0.12.0, is removed with no behaviour
change because it never ran. And an "unused" import that was a re-export
(specfiles.LICENSING_CSV) broke collection before being restored.

Known and deliberately not fixed here: whoami reports owned namespaces only,
not the union with membership. Not an authorization defect — every gate runs
through effective_role, which reads membership and the org cascade directly.
Widening it changes what an existing response field contains, which is
minor-sized under this project's own rule. Reasoning sits beside
effective_role in api/deps.py.

Client surface: unchanged. Suite 417 green on 0.6.1/0.6.1/0.6.4.

MAKING THE ROOT SUITES RUNNABLE. The four root e2e suites were skipped and therefore proved
nothing. Two independent omissions kept them dead. They gated on PROTEUS_AUTH, an AI Gateway
token, which is the one credential this account does not need: the default model is native
Workers AI DeepSeek, and a deployed worker already fronts it at /api/user/ai/v1 for any CLI
bearer. And the root `tests/` directory was typechecked by NOTHING: `bun run check` named
eight projects and not one included it.

Pointed at the project compiler for the first time, `tests/` produced 23 errors, calls to
APIs deleted months ago. The worst is `BuiltinToolDeps.engine`, passed at 9 call sites and
silently ignored at runtime, so every one of these suites built its toolset with evolution
NOT WIRED and then asserted on evolution events. Also `EvolutionEngine.onTurnComplete` (now
`reviewTurn`), `EvolutionConfig.sessionReflectionInterval`/`turnCraftThreshold`,
`SessionWriter.compact`, `WorkspaceInfo.id`, and `generateText({maxSteps})`. Setting a token
on the tree as it stood would have produced a red suite, not evidence. A permanently-skipped
test is not merely unproven, it decays, and the decay is invisible until someone tries to run
it.

- `resolveLiveModel` resolves a target from PROTEUS_ORIGIN + PROTEUS_TOKEN (the worker proxy,
  native Workers AI) or AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL + AI_GATEWAY_AUTH. A HALF-set environment returns
  `misconfigured` and THROWS: partial config used to resolve to an empty auth header and a
  silent skip.
- No hardcoded gateway URL. The four suites each carried the same account id in a fallback
  default; a public repo should not, and a harness that silently falls back cannot state which
  target it measured.
- One `liveChatModel` via core's `createChatModel`, so live runs inherit `withRateLimitRetry`.
  The four hand-rolled providers did not, making a mid-run 429 read as a behavioural failure.
- `recordLiveModelSpend`/`reportLiveModelSpend` measure what a run cost. Cost per run is not a
  constant when the model may take 500 steps.
- All 23 type errors repaired against current APIs with no assertion weakened. The single
  removed `expect` is `info.id`, whose invariant the adjacent
  `expect(rt2.identity.id).toBe(agentId)` already asserts.
- `tests/tsconfig.json`, wired into `bun run check`. The tsconfig is not the fix; `check`
  running it is.

Counts unchanged: 3 pass, 19 skip, 0 fail, 26 expect() calls.

THE RICH SCORERS. Three scorers, each reading through the PRODUCTION reader and each
reporting how many eligible things it looked at, separately from how many passed.

- `scoreExploration`: competed runs, of those how many opened more than ONE branch, how many
  the reader can hand a winning score for, and how many had that ranking survive into the
  store as exactly one terminal node. A run can return a `winnerId` in memory while no row was
  ever marked: ranked to the caller, unranked to every later reader.
- `scoreSettleVisibility`: for each settle mode's write store, does `listForkRuns` (what the
  Exploration pane calls) return what was written. Asks the reader for more rows than were
  written, because it slices AFTER merging its two halves, so its own window must never look
  like a missing row.
- `scoreDelegation`: per-arm {eligible, converted, rate} over `turn_steering`, never pooled:
  the step-25 arm only fires on turns the turn-start arm did not convert. `rate` is null for
  an empty arm, not 0; a rate over no turns is absent, not zero.

Two false zeros were caught inside the harness itself before it shipped. `scoreDelegation`
was first written against `tool_call_start` rows naming the `agents` tool. NO production code
emits that event type on either backend, the sinks emit `tool_call_end` and `step_finish`, so
it would have reported "never delegated" forever, on every run, and been believed. It now
counts `head_split`, which is what a fork actually writes, and a regression test pins the
shape. `alternate_takes` also has no `root_id` column, so the take lookup joins back through
`search_nodes`; a `WHERE root_id = …` would have matched nothing.

Every scorer has an empty-store test asserting a ZERO denominator rather than a pass, and
`scoreSettleVisibility` takes its reader as a seam so its negative controls can hand it the
reader AS IT WAS when the bug shipped, one that reads a single half, in both directions.
Today's reader returns any root in either store, so without that the green result would be
indistinguishable from a scorer that never looks. 18 tests, credential-free.

The live evals (tests/evals/) assert those scores against a real target: exploration drives
the fork through the real `agents` tool so the model cannot decline, and delegation drives
three FRESH workspaces through the full LocalAgentSession turn spine, because the turn-start
predicate needs a fresh ask, so N turns in one session would give a denominator of 1 while
looking like N. Its prompts are imperatives because the predicate refuses anything ending in
? or !. The denominator is asserted exactly; the RATE is reported, not gated, because at this
sample size a floor is a coin flip dressed as a gate.

THE EIGHT-SCORER PANEL. The reward signal CL-Bench found missing. Its first run recorded 14
evolution events in 14 turns, every one "ungraded (no follow-up) | 0 tool calls", ending at
scaffoldVersion 0 / craftedToolCount 0: evolution fired with nothing to learn from. These are
the instruments that grade a turn.

A uniform BehaviourScorer panel sits beside the three rich scorers, reading what the harness
already records: steering conversion across all five triggers, the craft loop closing
(crafted → reused), edits landing, recovery findings that HELD, completion honesty, spill
retrieval, and tool outcomes. Every one carries an explicit denominator and reports rate=null,
never 0, when nothing was eligible, because 0/0 is a fact about the task and 0/7 is a fact
about the agent.

Three of these needed their obvious form rejected:

  - recovery_durability over recoveries is a tautology: the event exists only when a streak
    was already broken, so n/n = 1.00 forever. Scored instead over the producer's own named
    falsifier, a signature recovered twice necessarily failed again.
  - completion_honesty inverts polarity. converted=true means the gate caught a premature
    completion claim, so the numerator is the UN-converted rows. Scored the obvious way round
    it would reward declaring victory early.
  - spill_retrieval excludes spills with no resolvable address. There was nothing to read
    back, so charging it to the agent scores our defect.

Exports parseStoredRunEvent, the canonical parse RunEventRecorder already uses, and reads
through it, which deleted seven local interfaces copying shapes the producer owns. Type
narrowing is in SQL, unlike the recorder's own reader, so one malformed row costs one number
instead of all eight. That switch also caught the fixture: it wrote only type-specific fields
while production persists the whole stamped event, so every json_extract scorer read it
happily while the canonical parse rejected it, the write/read disagreement this module's
docstring warns about, inside its own tests.

41/41 green. Each scorer has a pass, a RED on the defect it exists for, and a
zero-denominator case; a trigger outside the producer's picklist is pinned to throw rather
than quietly leave the denominator.

THE GATES. Two gates for the same defect class, both found by trying to run tests nobody had
run: a signal that is missing is indistinguishable from a signal that is fine, unless
something asserts the corpus was non-empty.

`gate:skip-ratchet` locks the SET of skipped tests, with a written reason per entry.
`bun test ./tests/` reports 23 skips and exits 0, and the exit code is all anyone reads.
Locking the set rather than a count is the point: a count of 23 cannot tell you a different 23
are skipping now. It also fails when a locked skip starts running, so the ratchet only
tightens; and it asserts every target contributed a test, because `bun test tests` and
`bun test tests/` both match NOTHING here and only `./tests/` selects them. `--lock`
deliberately refuses to write: a reason is not something a script can generate.

`gate:typecheck-coverage` derives the project list from the `check` script, following
`bun run` transitively, without which it demands an exclusion for `tools/oxlint/anti-slop`,
which IS covered, and compares it against every directory on disk holding a `*.test.ts`. The
root `tests/` directory was covered by nothing, which is how four suites came to call two
deleted APIs. Both sides must be non-empty or `assertMeasured` kills the run.

Both gates have their own tests, 23 of them, including the one that matters most: a JUnit
parse matching only self-closing `<testcase/>` elements reports every SKIPPED test as absent,
so the ratchet would reconcile an empty set and pass forever.

`test:eval` is the tier. It names the target and cost basis BEFORE spending anything, runs the
suites once, enforces the ratchet over THAT report rather than a second run, and prints the
measured spend. With no credentials it still runs and still passes, because a tier nobody can
reproduce without a secret is not a tier, while the ratchet stays mandatory. Targets are
root-relative because `bun test --cwd` does not read the root bunfig.toml and silently loses
both the throwaway PROTEUS_HOME and pathIgnorePatterns. Cost is reported as measured model
calls and tokens, never dollars: a price is a platform number and the catalog carries limits,
not prices.

Wired into LADDER (commit / push / ci) and deploy.sh, keeping the two in the same order;
deploy.test.ts asserts exact equality. The existing ci `bun test ./tests/` entry keeps its
place but its text was wrong on all three counts it claimed (22 tests, 19 skips,
PROTEUS_AUTH); its `blind` now names what it cannot see, a suite whose code no longer
compiles, because bun strips types.

DEPENDENCIES. package.json resolves to main's side, strictly newer on both blocks:
root-relative `bun test packages/*/` over the old `--cwd` spelling, plus test:workerd, the
cf-backend/tests/workerd typecheck project and the no-ambient-git gate. vitest-evals is pinned
exactly. 0.x with 30 releases and two root-API reshapes already: the scorer-first
`describeEval({data, task, scorers})` moved to `vitest-evals/legacy` at 0.9.0, so a caret
range would silently change API. Peer is vitest >=4 <5 and we are on 4.1.10, which
pool-workers 0.21.3 also peers, so one vitest serves both pools.

MODELS, verified against the account's own catalogue rather than derived from each other; the
suffixes differ and a guess would have been wrong:

  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROTEUS_TOKEN" $PROTEUS_ORIGIN/api/user/ai/v1/models
    pro    @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813    (= DEFAULT_WORKERS_AI_MODEL_ID)
    flash  @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731  (exposed and serving)

Both answered real completions. A two-point measurement at fixed prompt puts pro at exactly
3.0x flash per token on both coefficients, which turns "flash for volume, pro for bounds" into
a budget; a run record declares which regime made it.

WHAT MAKES A RUN EVIDENCE. `assessAdmissibility` refuses to call a run a measurement without
graded turns, tool calls, at least one scorer with a non-zero denominator, and an executed
task set equal to the declared one. The last is the measured-set/governed-set equality as an
assertion; the first two are what CL-Bench lacked when it reported mean_gain -0.2 over a
corpus whose every turn was "ungraded | 0 tool calls" with 500 steps available and one used.

WHY THE HARNESS THROWS, the load-bearing decision. vitest-evals writes task.meta.eval from
applyAutomaticJudges (dist/index.mjs:1393) and from appendJudgeScore, the explicit
toSatisfyJudge path (:1447). Both are reachable only from a result run(...) handed back;
clearRecordedTaskMeta (:1229) blanks the metadata first; the catch path writes only
meta.harness before rethrowing. So a throwing harness publishes no score, whereas an expect()
in the test body runs after both writers: at :1393 the write is unconditional and the
threshold assert fires afterwards, so the number is published first and the failure raised
second. Choosing between automatic and explicit judges is not a fix: the surface is any judge
that scores on a degenerate run.

Proven on the emitted JSON both ways, with a control exercising the path the case must avoid:
  healthy     passed  meta.eval PRESENT avg=1  meta.harness present
  degenerate  failed  meta.eval ABSENT         meta.harness present
The control is not decoration: with the precondition throwing in both fixtures, "does not
publish" and "never ran" predict the same observation and the test cannot discriminate.

RUNNER: one vitest config scoped to tests/evals/**/*.eval.ts, disjoint from `bun test` by FILE
EXTENSION rather than a second bunfig ignore pattern, so the four existing bun eval suites
stay put and ladder.ts's TEST_FILE regex cannot see these files. It must run under
`bun --bun`: the spine opens the agent store through bun:sqlite, and node-hosted vitest
collects ZERO tests, which would read as a clean tier. Replay is off and .vitest-evals/
gitignored: recordings capture tool INPUT verbatim, which for an agent harness is where a
bearer lives. Corpus is additive: seed.jsonl untouched, its no-tool cases filtered by tag,
because a task that hands over no environment cannot exercise any mechanism.

Also fixes a defect the panel shipped with: tool_outcomes counted only the transport `error`
flag, so a command that ran and exited non-zero, an ordinary successful result whose text
begins `Error (exit N)`, scored as clean. Adds isFailingResultText beside formatExecResult,
the renderer that writes that prefix, as the one definition. The same confusion graded a
command exiting 3 as `accepted` at quality 0.70 in the evolution reward: the worst call in the
turn contributing the best number.

84/84 across test-utils and the artifact contract; `bun run check` exit 0.

THE FIRST LIVE RECORDS. 36 episodes against @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 through
the deployed worker proxy, the first live-model behavioural measurement this project has. The
two records here are the paired flash runs; both are ADMISSIBLE.

  flash-a  14 graded turns, 126 tool calls, 2,623,902 in / 59,796 out
  flash-b  13 graded turns, 113 tool calls, 2,199,758 in / 50,427 out
  delegation_conversion  0.154 / 0.167     steering_conversion 0.143 / 0.167
  edit_landing           1.000 / 1.000     tool_outcomes       0.817 / 0.903
  craft_reuse, completion_honesty, spill_retrieval: NO eligible opportunity

That last line is the point of the denominator discipline. Three mechanisms were never
exercised by this corpus, and they report absent rather than zero: "could not" is a fact about
the tasks, "did not" is a fact about the agent, and collapsing them is how a corpus that never
reached a mechanism comes to read as an agent that never uses it.

The comparison refuses to overclaim. Every scorer whose paired tasks differed fewer than 6
times leads with UNDECIDABLE and prints the floor from the DIFFERING count, not the task
count. tool_outcomes moved +5.9pp with CI [+2.0pp, +9.9pp] and is still UNDECIDABLE: only 4 of
6 paired tasks differed, so the best two-sided p reachable is 0.1250. That is the exact error
CL-Bench made when it read a -20pp gain whose true floor was p=0.5 over 2 differing pairs.
recovery_durability is reported as a change in what the corpus REACHED rather than a
behavioural delta, because it had an opportunity in one run and none in the other.

Both records carry the arm state (evolution ON, settle none, 8 tools), the model id, the seed,
the repeat count and the git sha, and both are flagged DIRTY, honestly, since the tree carried
untracked scratch when they were produced. A record that cannot say what produced it is not
comparable.

**Root Cause**:

2. **MCP service readiness check**: Wait for MCP service to fully restart before proceeding
3. **Verification logging**: Add detailed logs to track permission verification and service status

**Key Changes**:
- Modified `handlePermissionResponse` to wait for permission config completion
- Added `waitForMcpServiceReady` method to ensure MCP service is ready
- Enhanced verification logging to track server permissions and service status
- Proper timing: Permission grant → MCP restart → Service ready → Agent loop restart

This ensures that when the agent loop restarts, all permissions are properly configured and MCP services are fully operational, preventing tool call failures due to timing issues.
